opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it really goes back to how diffusion models were originally developed. They were designed for continuous data like images, audio, and video, where the pixel values live in a continuous space. The whole idea is that you start from clean data, gradually add Gaussian noise until you get pure noise, and then train a neural network to reverse that process step by step. That works beautifully when you can add a little bit of noise to a pixel value and get something that's still meaningful, just slightly perturbed.

With text and code, there's no natural notion of adding a little Gaussian noise to a token. A word is either "cat" or "dog." You can't have something that's 0.3 of the way between them in any meaningful sense. So the core mathematical machinery, the forward noising process, the score function, which is the gradient of the log density, doesn't directly carry over. Gradients don't really make sense on a discrete space.

People tried workarounds early on, like embedding tokens into a continuous space and diffusing there, and then rounding back to the nearest token at the end. That kind of works, but it's clunky, and the rounding step introduces errors. Performance lagged quite a bit behind autoregressive models.

So a big part of our research was figuring out the right generalization of diffusion to discrete spaces. Instead of the score, we looked at ratios of probabilities between neighboring sequences, what we called concrete scores, and developed a way to learn them, score entropy. The noising process becomes something like randomly masking or replacing tokens, and the model learns to undo that corruption. Once you get the math right, discrete diffusion becomes competitive with autoregressive models on quality, and you get the advantages diffusion has always had: generating many tokens in parallel, being much faster at inference, and being more controllable, since you're not locked into strict left-to-right generation. That's what made us excited enough to try to commercialize it.

r001.rationale: It says a small amount of noise added to a pixel can leave the image meaningful and slightly perturbed.

r002.rationale: It explains that there is no meaningful way to move partway between discrete words such as “cat” and “dog.”

r003.rationale: It says there is no natural Gaussian noise to add to tokens, so the continuous-space noising machinery does not directly apply to text and code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, and it really gets at the heart of why diffusion for language took longer to work than diffusion for images.

If you think about how diffusion models work in the image domain, the whole framework is built around the idea of adding Gaussian noise. You take an image, which is just a big vector of continuous pixel values, and you gradually corrupt it by adding small amounts of noise, step by step, until you end up with pure noise. Then you train a neural network to reverse that process, to denoise a little bit at a time. And the reason that works so beautifully is that everything is continuous. You can add a tiny bit of noise, you can compute gradients, you can take small steps in the direction of the data distribution. The math is very clean because it's essentially all built on calculus over real-valued spaces.

Now, text and code don't look like that at all. A sentence is a sequence of tokens, and each token is one element from a vocabulary of, say, fifty thousand or a hundred thousand discrete symbols. There's no natural notion of adding "a little bit of noise" to the word "cat." What does it mean to perturb a token by epsilon? You can't move a tiny fraction of the way from "cat" to "dog." Either it's "cat" or it's something else. So the core primitive that diffusion relies on, this smooth, gradual corruption process, just doesn't have an obvious analog in a discrete space.

People have tried a few workarounds. One approach is to embed the tokens into a continuous space, run standard Gaussian diffusion there, and then round back to the nearest token at the end. And that can work to some degree, but it's kind of awkward. You're forcing the problem into a shape it doesn't really want to be in, and you lose a lot of efficiency because the model spends capacity learning about regions of the embedding space that don't correspond to any real token.

The other direction, which is the one I find more principled, is to redefine the forward process itself to be discrete. Instead of adding Gaussian noise, you corrupt tokens by, say, masking them or randomly replacing them with other tokens, according to some transition matrix. Then the reverse process becomes a model that predicts what the original tokens were, given a partially corrupted sequence. Conceptually that's very natural, but it brings its own challenges. The score function, which is the thing you estimate in continuous diffusion, is a gradient, and gradients don't exist over discrete states. So you have to figure out what the right analog is, something like estimating ratios of probabilities between neighboring states rather than derivatives. Getting the training objective right, getting it to be stable and to scale, that's been a lot of the research effort.

And there's also the question of what you gain. The reason this matters at all is that autoregressive models, the GPT-style models, are extremely good at text. They generate one token at a time, left to right, and that's a very natural fit for the sequential, discrete nature of language. So diffusion has to earn its place. The promise is that you get parallel generation, you get the ability to do iterative refinement, to edit and go back and fix mistakes, to condition on things in a more flexible way. But to realize that promise, you first have to solve this foundational mismatch between a framework built for continuous data and a domain that is fundamentally made of symbols.

r001.rationale: The response says images have continuous pixel values and can receive small amounts of noise, but it does not explain that those changes generally preserve an image’s meaning.

r002.rationale: It says there is no natural way to move a fraction of the way from one token, such as “cat,” to another, such as “dog.”

r003.rationale: It explains that text has no obvious analog to gradual noise corruption, making the noise process required by diffusion unclear for discrete tokens.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that diffusion models are very natural for continuous data. With an image, for example, you can add a little bit of Gaussian noise to the pixel values, then a little bit more, and gradually turn the image into pure noise. You train a model to reverse that process, taking small steps back toward a clean image.

With text or code, it’s less clear what that small perturbation should be. A token is a discrete object. You can replace it with another token, or mask it out, but you can’t really change it by an arbitrarily small amount. And changing just one token can have a very large effect on the meaning of a sentence or whether a piece of code is valid.

So you have to rethink the corruption process and how you learn to reverse it. You could work in a continuous embedding space, but then you have to map back to discrete tokens. Or you can define diffusion directly over discrete states. Neither is impossible, but the choices that work so well for images don’t transfer quite as directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes adding small Gaussian noise to image pixels, but does not say that small pixel-color changes generally preserve an image’s meaning.

r002.rationale: It says tokens are discrete and cannot be changed by an arbitrarily small amount, clearly conveying the lack of natural interpolation between tokens.

r003.rationale: It explains that for text or code it is less clear what a small perturbation should be because tokens are discrete, conveying why the noise process for denoising is unclear.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that diffusion models are very naturally defined for continuous data. With an image, for example, you can add a little bit of Gaussian noise to the pixel values, then a little bit more, and train a model to reverse that process. You have this smooth progression from a clean image to noise.

With text or code, what does it mean to add a little bit of noise to a token? You can replace a word or mask it out, but those are discrete changes, and even a single change can have a big effect on meaning or whether a program is valid. So the machinery that works so well in continuous spaces doesn’t transfer directly.

You can either move into a continuous representation, like embeddings, and eventually map back to tokens, or design a diffusion process that operates directly on discrete symbols. Both are possible, but you have to think carefully about the corruption process and how to learn its reverse. That’s what makes it an interesting modeling challenge.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradually adding Gaussian noise to image pixels, but does not say that small pixel changes generally preserve an image’s meaning.

r002.rationale: It says token changes are discrete and can affect meaning, but does not identify the absence of a natural, meaningful interpolation between tokens.

r003.rationale: It notes that defining token corruption requires care, but does not explain this in terms of text lacking a natural geometry.
